headline: Suji is possibly す (*su) plus ち (chi, “life essence, spirit, power; blood; milk”), with chi voiced to ji by rendaku.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *suntuy ~ *sunti.

Possibly a compound of す (*su, unknown, possibly the same source as 脛(すね) (sune, “shin”)) + 霊(ち), 血(ち), 乳(ち) (chi, “life essence, spirit, power; blood; milk”), with the chi changing to ji due to rendaku (連濁).

headline: Kojin is a calque of English individual, listed in the 1912 Ei-Doku-Futsu-Wa Tetsugaku Jii.

sources.quote: Short for 一(いっ)個(こ)人(じん) (ikkojin) or 各(かく)個(こ)人(じん) (kakukojin), from 一(いっ)個(こ)の人(ひと) (ikko no hito), a calque of English individual.
Listed in the 1912 work 英独仏和哲学字彙 (Ei-Doku-Futsu-Wa Tetsugaku Jii, “Dictionary of English, German, and French Philosophical Terms”) as a translation of English individual.

headline: Hau is written with 這, a kokkun not derived from the Chinese kanbun tradition.

sources.quote: The usage of the character 這 is considered to be a 国訓 (kokkun) not derived from Chinese 漢文 (kanbun) tradition. Alongside China's usage of the character 這 /这 for a medieval pronoun, also of murky origins, this makes 這 a character with markedly different usages in both countries/languages. It is possibly a corrupt form of 𧥡, which is an ancient form of 誕 (MC danX) and borrowed as 蜒 (MC yen).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 沿ふ (sopu). Used in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.

headline: Itsumademo is いつ (itsu, “when”) plus まで (made, “until, up to”) plus も (mo, “even, also”): literally “until even any time”.

sources.quote: From いつ (itsu, “when”) + まで (made, “until, up to”) + も (mo, “even, also”, inclusive) Literally, "until even any time".

The construction itsu made ("until when") is attested already as Old Japanese itu made in the Man'yōshū of 759 CE. Likewise, the construction made mo ("even until") is also attested in the Man'yōshū, as is itu mo ("any time, whenever; always"). That said, the earliest attestation of the full phrase itsu made mo might not be until the Shaku Nihongi in the late 1200s.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 癥狀 (MC tring dzrjangH, “abdominal tumor, disease + form, appearance”)). Compare modern simplified Chinese 症状 (zhèngzhuàng, “symptom”).

headline: Nayamu appears in the Man'yōshū of 759 and may derive from 萎える (naeru, “to weaken; to wither”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Appears in the Man'yōshū completed in 759 CE.
May be derived from 萎える (naeru, “to weaken; to wither; to bend; to become limp; to become listless”), from the classical form 萎ゆ (nayu) in the irrealis verb stem naya- + suppositional suffix む (mu).

headline: Soto appears from roughly the Muromachi period, likely 背 (so, “back, behind”) plus 外 (to, “outside”) or 所 (to, “place”).

sources.quote: Appears from roughly the Muromachi period, superseding earlier to reading (see below). Likely a compound of either 背 (so, “back, behind”, ancient reading found in compounds) + 外 (to, “outside”), or 背 (so, “back, behind”, ancient reading found in compounds) + 所 (to, “place”).

headline: Hara, “field”, is compared with Middle Korean ᄇᆞᆯ (pól), whence modern 벌 (beol).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Found in the Man'yōshū, finished some time after 759 CE. Compare Middle Korean ᄇᆞᆯ〮 (pól, “field, plain”), whence modern 벌 (beol). Possibly from 原(はる) (haru) below, by vowel assimilation.

sources.quote: Reduplication of the archaic adverb いよ (iyo, “more and more, increasingly”), shift of いや (iya, “more and more, increasingly”), in turn from the prefix い (i-) and the adverb や (ya, “more and more, increasingly”).

sources.quote: ⟨mawosu⟩ → */mawusu/ → /mausu/ → /mɔːsu/ → /moːsu/

meaning: to hate, to dislike, to loathe
headline: Kirau is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE; the Daijiten lists it as cognate with 切る (kiru, “to cut”), but Samuel Martin thinks that unlikely.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Listed in the Daijiten as being cognate with 切る (kiru, “to cut”), perhaps via ふ (fu, repetitive verb suffix). However, Samuel Martin thinks this is unlikely.

headline: Terasu is originally the causative of 照る (teru, “to shine”): “to make shine”.

sources.quote: Originally the causative of 照(て)る (teru, “to shine”), from 照(て)ら (tera, the 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of 照(て)る (teru)) + す (-su, classical causative auxiliary, originally with 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”); modern せる (seru)), hence “to make shine”.

headline: Nodo, “throat”, may come from nomito: 飲み (nomi, “to drink”) plus 門 (to, “gate, door”).

sources.quote: ⟨no₂mi₁ to₁⟩ → */nəmʲitʷo/ → /nomʉto//nomʉdo/ → /nondo/ → /nodo/
Shift from 喉(のんど) (nondo), ultimately from 喉(のみと) (nomito), a compound of 飲み (nomi, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 飲む (nomu), “to drink”) + 門 (to, “gate, door”).
